{{Short description|Finite group}}
[[File:Cayley graph of the quasidihedral group of order 16.svg|thumb|[[Cayley graph]] of the quasidihedral group of order 16]]
[[File:Cayley graph of the modular maximal-cyclic group of order 16.svg|thumb|Cayley graph of the modular maximal-cyclic group of order 16]]
[[File:Cayley graph of the dihedral group of order 16.svg|thumb|Cayley graph of the dihedral group of order 16]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''quasi-dihedral groups''', also called  '''semi-dihedral groups''', are certain [[non-abelian group]]s of [[order (group theory)|order]] a power of 2.  For every positive [[integer]] ''n'' greater than or equal to 4, there are exactly four [[isomorphism class]]es of non-abelian [[group (mathematics)|group]]s of order 2<sup>''n''</sup> which have a [[cyclic group|cyclic]] [[subgroup]] of [[Index of a subgroup|index]] 2.  Two are well known, the [[generalized quaternion group]] and the [[dihedral group]]. One of the remaining two groups is often considered particularly important, since it is an example of a 2-group of [[maximal class|maximal nilpotency class]].  In [[Bertram Huppert]]'s text ''Endliche Gruppen'', this group is called a "Quasidiedergruppe".  In [[Daniel Gorenstein]]'s text, ''Finite Groups'', this group is called the "semidihedral group". Dummit and Foote refer to it as the "quasidihedral group"; we adopt that name in this article. All give the same [[group presentation|presentation]] for this group:

:<math>\langle r,s \mid r^{2^{n-1}} = s^2 = 1,\ srs = r^{2^{n-2}-1}\rangle\,\!</math>.

The other non-abelian 2-group with cyclic subgroup of index 2 is not given a special name in either text, but referred to as just ''G'' or M<sub>''m''</sub>(2). When this group has order 16, Dummit and Foote refer to this group as the "modular group of order 16", as its [[Iwasawa group|lattice of subgroups is modular]].  In this article this group will be called the modular maximal-cyclic group of order <math>2^n</math>. Its presentation is:

:<math>\langle r,s \mid r^{2^{n-1}} = s^2 = 1,\ srs = r^{2^{n-2}+1}\rangle\,\!</math>.

Both these two groups and the dihedral group are [[semidirect product]]s of a cyclic group <''r''> of order 2<sup>''n''−1</sup> with a cyclic group <''s''> of order 2.  Such a non-abelian semidirect product is uniquely determined by an element of order 2 in the [[group of units]] of the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>\mathbb{Z}/2^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}</math> and there are precisely three such elements, <math>2^{n-1}-1</math>, <math>2^{n-2}-1</math>, and <math>2^{n-2}+1</math>, corresponding to the dihedral group, the quasidihedral, and the modular maximal-cyclic group.

The generalized quaternion group, the dihedral group, and the quasidihedral group of order 2<sup>''n''</sup> all have nilpotency class ''n'' − 1, and are the only isomorphism classes of groups of order 2<sup>''n''</sup> with nilpotency class ''n'' − 1.  The groups of order ''p''<sup>''n''</sup> and nilpotency class ''n'' − 1 were the beginning of the classification of all [[p-group|''p''-groups]] via [[p-group#Classification|coclass]].  The modular maximal-cyclic group of order 2<sup>''n''</sup> always has nilpotency class 2.  This makes the modular maximal-cyclic group less interesting, since most groups of order ''p''<sup>''n''</sup> for large ''n'' have nilpotency class 2 and have proven difficult to understand directly. <!-- I need to go get a copy of this folklore statement. the result should be in {{MR|113948}} or {{MR|169921}} -->

The generalized quaternion, the dihedral, and the quasidihedral group are the only 2-groups whose [[derived subgroup]] has index 4.  The [[Alperin–Brauer–Gorenstein theorem]] classifies the [[simple group]]s, and to a degree the [[finite group]]s, with quasidihedral Sylow 2-subgroups.

==Examples==

The Sylow 2-subgroups of the following groups are quasidihedral:
*PSL<sub>3</sub>('''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>) for ''q'' ≡ 3 mod 4,
*PSU<sub>3</sub>('''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>) for ''q'' ≡ 1 mod 4,
*the [[Mathieu group]] M<sub>11</sub>,
*GL<sub>2</sub>('''F'''<sub>''q''</sub>) for ''q'' ≡ 3 mod 4.
